Altrata  ·  Advanced Search
I was asked to add OR logic to one filter. After researching how customers actually built searches, I argued for a reusable logic model across the entire Advanced Search experience.

Its Advanced Search capability is central to customers across fundraising, wealth management, investment banking and executive search, where users turn millions of records into actionable prospect lists.

The problem
A parity ticket exposed a bigger limitation in Advanced Search

The work started as a migration parity ticket. As clients from RelSci, Wealth-X and BoardEx were being consolidated into Altrata, one identified gap was the lack of Boolean logic within the Location filter.

Before designing it, I reviewed how the same capability worked across the three foundational products. All three had solved the problem in roughly the same way: Boolean logic existed in Location, but stopped there.
Replicating that behaviour would have closed the parity gap. It would also have carried the same limitation into Altrata.
The deeper issue was the search model itself.

Advanced Search treated every filter as part of one flat query. Conditions across Location, Role, Experience, Education and other modules were implicitly combined using AND logic, but that relationship was neither visible nor editable.
This worked for simple and straightforward searches:
CEO · London · Financial Services
But not for the way many clients actually defined a target group needed to express a more realistic set of criteria:
CEO OR CTO · based in Washington or New York · works for a New York-based company · excluding existing clients

The product could narrow a list, but it could not express alternatives or exclusions. To complete a search like this, users had to split the logic across multiple searches, exports and manual filtering outside Altrata.
At that point, the question was no longer simply “how should AND / OR work in Location?”
It became:
Is Location really the only place clients need Boolean logic, or simply the first place the limitation became visible?
Understanding how clients were actually using search
I looked across verticals before asking for a wider scope

Direct client research would take longer than the parity timeline allowed, so I first worked with the people closest to client behaviour: account managers, client success, commercial teams and colleagues who had worked with these customer groups for years.

I treated this as directional evidence rather than a substitute for client research. The goal at this stage was not to validate a solution; it was to understand whether the limitation was genuinely broader than Location.
Across different verticals, the search intent varied, but the underlying need was consistent.
Nonprofit and education teams were building prospect lists around affinity, giving history and wealth, often needing to include several criteria while excluding prospects already assigned elsewhere.
Wealth and financial services teams were looking across multiple geographies and wealth bands, while excluding existing clients.
Investment banking teams were identifying decision-makers across equivalent titles, sectors and organisations.
Executive search researchers were building candidate pools from combinations of titles, industries and experience, then excluding adjacent but irrelevant profiles.
Healthcare teams were combining geography, affinity and capacity while removing restricted or previously contacted individuals.
Different users were applying different filters, but they were repeatedly trying to do the same three things:
combine alternatives, intersect criteria, and exclude exceptions.
Location was not the boundary of the problem. It was simply where the problem was most visible.
The real workflow extended beyond Altrata
Advanced Search could narrow a list, but users were finishing the logic elsewhere
The conversations also exposed a shared workflow.
Clients rarely arrived with a fully formed query. They started broad, inspected the results, and progressively refined the list until it was specific enough to act on.
The flat search model supported part of that process, but not all of it.
When the logic became more complex, teams were compensating manually.
Search, export, merge
A request containing two acceptable alternatives often became two separate searches and two exports, followed by a manual merge.
Exclusions done by deletion
An exclusion became a larger search first, followed by deleting unwanted records against another list.
Finish it in another system
In some cases, users deliberately ran a loose search in Altrata and completed the real filtering in Excel or their own internal systems.
That changed the framing of the problem for me.
The issue was not simply that Advanced Search was missing an operator. It was that Altrata was handing users part of the workflow, then forcing them outside the product to finish it.
That also explained the repeated search-and-export patterns observed by client-facing teams when supporting complex client requests.
Widening the scope
I framed the decision around the cost of solving the same problem twice
The original request was still the fastest option: add AND / OR to Location and close the migration gap.

But by this point, we had enough evidence to expect the same need to surface elsewhere — through future tickets, account managers and client feedback around roles, experience, education and other filters.
Solving it only in Location would create three costs.
First, design and engineering rework. We would build a one-off interaction now, then revisit the logic, UI and underlying implementation each time another module needed the same capability.
Second, product inconsistency. One filter would behave differently from the rest of Advanced Search, making the experience harder to understand and harder to scale.

Third, a user expectation we would later have to change. Once clients learned that Boolean logic worked in a particular way inside Location, expanding it across the rest of the product could mean changing a mental model we had just taught them.
So I brought product and engineering a broader alternative: define one logic model for Advanced Search now, then apply it consistently across modules.

It meant spending more time upfront, but it reduced future redesign and rebuild work, kept the interaction model coherent, and gave us a foundation that could accommodate the next request without turning it into another standalone project.
The decision was therefore not simply “ship now or make the UX better.” It was:
Do we optimise for the quickest parity fix, or use this moment to establish the model we are likely to need anyway?
We aligned on the broader direction, while keeping the scope controlled: the existing Advanced Search structure would stay intact. We were extending its logic, not redesigning the product.
That became the new brief:
Introduce Boolean logic across Advanced Search in a way that scales across modules without making simple searches harder.
Constraint check
I tested the boundaries before designing the interaction

Once the wider scope was agreed, I sat down with the engineering lead and data team before moving into concepts. The goal was to separate interface limitations from platform limitations early, avoiding designs that would later require rework.
Four constraints shaped the solution.

The engine already supported Boolean logic AND, OR and NOT could already be executed by the underlying search engine. The limitation was not in the platform capability; it was in how Advanced Search exposed that capability to users.
This shifted the design question from:“Can we build this?”to:“How should this complexity be represented in an experience that remains approachable?”

Boolean relationships could extend beyond Location The technical architecture did not limit Boolean logic to a single filter. Conditions could be combined across areas such as Role, Location and Experience, so I kept cross-module logic open rather than reproducing the limitation of the foundational products.

Nesting needed a ceiling Unlimited nested groups would require a different query structure and additional backend changes and was outside the delivery window. We therefore kept the logic shallow rather than supporting arbitrary nested parentheses.

This was not only a technical constraint. Deeply nested queries are also harder for users to interpret, validate and recover from. A user should be able to understand the logic behind a prospect list without having to decode multiple layers of brackets.

Existing search behaviour had to remain intact Boolean logic had the potential to improve search across the customer base, but it also introduced more complexity into an interaction users already knew.
The experience therefore needed to support two levels of behaviour:
•	keeping straightforward searches simple and familiar;
•	giving power users enough control to express complex criteria when needed.
The goal was not to replace the existing search model, but to extend it without increasing friction for everyday workflows.

Saved searches introduced a later dependency Saved searches introduced one further technical dependency: the existing schema stored a flat set of filters, so persisting a Boolean query would require additional backend work.
Rather than allowing this dependency to block the core experience, we captured it as a future enhancement and focused the first release on query creation, editing and execution.

By the end of the review, the design space had clear edges: Boolean logic across modules was technically viable, unlimited nesting was not, and the existing search experience needed to remain the foundation.
The next question was no longer whether Boolean logic belonged in Advanced Search. It was How visible and structured should that logic be?
Two concepts
I explored two different ways of containing the complexity
The technical review confirmed Boolean logic could work across Advanced Search. The harder product question was:
Where should that complexity live?
I saw two viable directions, representing two different product strategies.

One could preserve the existing Advanced Search model and reveal Boolean controls progressively inside it. The other could make complex logic explicit by giving users a dedicated space to construct and inspect a query.

Rather than converging early, I developed both far enough to test the trade-off properly. I wanted the concepts to answer different hypotheses, not simply offer two visual treatments of the same interaction.
The decision would come down to four things:
•	how much familiarity we could preserve;
•	how easily users could understand and verify the logic they created;
•	how each approach scaled as queries became more complex;
•	whether users felt confident that the final results represented their intent.
Concept A — a dedicated logic builder
The first concept treated Boolean logic as an advanced query construction layer.

Users could move from the familiar filter panel into a structured builder where each condition was represented explicitly and connected through AND or OR, with exclusions available at condition level.
The strategic advantage was explicit control and visibility.
Complex searches had a clear structure, allowing power users to inspect relationships between conditions and directly manipulate the query they were creating.

The trade-off was equally important: it introduced a second search model. Users would need to understand when to enter the builder, how it related to the standard filter experience, and how to interpret the structure they created.
The hypothesis behind Concept A was:
If users could explicitly see and control the query structure, they would have greater confidence when building complex searches, even if it introduced a new interaction model.
Concept B — extend the mental model users already have
The second concept kept users entirely inside the existing Advanced Search structure.
Rather than introducing a separate mode, I added Boolean controls contextually where relationships naturally occurred:
•	AND / OR between filter modules;
•	AND / OR between filters inside a module;
•	AND / OR between multiple values inside a filter;
•	NOT at value level after a value had been selected.

The rationale was to keep the logic close to the condition it affected. Operators were positioned beside the filters and values they controlled, using proximity and chunking to make relationships easier to interpret.
The strategic advantage was continuity.
Boolean logic became an extension of Advanced Search rather than a separate capability users had to discover and learn. The structure stayed connected to the objects users were already familiar with.
It also supported the principle established earlier:
Simple searches should remain simple, while more expressive controls should become available when users need them.

The trade-off was query visibility at scale. As searches became more complex, the logic could become distributed across multiple filters and modules. Users could build the query naturally, but understanding the complete relationship between conditions became harder.
The hypothesis behind Concept B was:
If Boolean logic was embedded into the existing workflow, users could gain more expressive search capability without needing to learn a different way of searching.
I prototyped behaviour, not just screens

I built both concepts as high-fidelity interactive prototypes in Claude Design. This allowed me to closely reproduce Altrata's design system and the behaviour of the live Advanced Search experience, making the concepts feel like realistic product extensions rather than standalone prototypes.

That mattered because the key questions were behavioural, not visual. Boolean logic only becomes meaningful through interaction: could users create a query, understand the relationships they had created, modify criteria and recover from mistakes?
Claude Design also enabled rapid iteration between research rounds, allowing concepts to evolve based on feedback without waiting for engineering implementation.
By the time we moved into testing, the prototypes were close enough to the live product that feedback focused on the interaction model and search logic, rather than prototype limitations.
At this stage, I was not trying to prove one concept was better. I wanted to understand the trade-off:
Should Advanced Search expose the structure of complex logic, or should it absorb that complexity into the interaction users already know?
Round 1 — stress-testing the interaction models
I used internal expertise to identify structural problems before involving clients
The first round was deliberately internal.
At this stage, I was not trying to validate the final direction with customers. I wanted to identify technical, interaction and usability risks early, while they were still inexpensive to change.

We tested with nine participants across Engineering, Data, Product and long-tenured team members who understood both the platform and the workflows that had developed around the foundational products.
Everyone tested both concepts through a within-subject study. To reduce order bias, we counterbalanced the sequence: half started with Concept A and half with Concept B.
Rather than asking participants to invent queries themselves, we provided realistic search scenarios so we could compare how each concept supported complex search tasks.
We measured:
•	ease of completing the search (SEQ);
•	confidence that the query represented the intended criteria;
•	overall preference.
The quantitative results were treated as directional rather than decisive. Ease scores were closely matched:
Concept A: 5.1/7 Concept B: 5.2/7
Preference was also relatively balanced:
Concept A: 4 Concept B: 5
The more valuable insights came from understanding where each interaction model created friction.
Concept B — too much visibility created too much noise
Concept B achieved the familiarity we wanted, but exposing Boolean relationships everywhere created unnecessary complexity.
The issue was not Boolean logic itself. It was that users had to understand which relationship each connector controlled.
Participants found value in Boolean logic within a clear context, such as multiple values inside one criterion:
CEO OR CTO and COO
However, relationships between different modules were harder to interpret:
Does this OR apply only between these two filters? Does it affect previous selections as well?
This showed that visibility alone does not create understanding. The relationship needs to appear where users can naturally interpret it.
For the next iteration, I kept the capability but reduced the initial cognitive load:
•	module-level operators appeared only when both modules contained active criteria;
•	filter-level operators appeared only when both filters were being used;
•	value-level operators appeared only after multiple values were selected.
This preserved flexibility while using proximity and chunking to keep relationships close to the conditions they affected.
Query visibility became as important as query construction

The sessions also surfaced a problem I hadn't given enough weight to: building the query was only half the job. Users also needed to verify what they had built. So it revealed a broader issue: creating a query and understanding a query were two different problems.

This was particularly visible in Concept B. Once Boolean relationships were distributed across several modules, checking the search meant moving back through the panel and reconstructing the logic mentally.

Participants repeatedly expressed the need for a clearer way to review the overall search logic before running the query. They wanted confidence that the criteria they had selected represented what they intended to find. Several also wanted all active filters reviewable without scrolling through the panel.
This led us to introduce a search summary in the next iteration.

The summary was designed as a verification layer between search creation and results. Instead of forcing users to reconstruct the logic from individual filters, it provided a single place to review the complete query and understand how the final prospect list was generated.
The principle we carried forward:
A powerful query is only valuable if users can understand and trust the query they created.
Concept A — structure was clear, but the interaction model was rigid
Concept A solved the visibility problem by making the query structure explicit, but the sessions exposed usability issues in how conditions were represented.
Participants expected related values from the same field to behave as a single logical group:
CEO OR CFO
rather than separate conditions requiring users to manually construct the relationship.
We also identified limitations around exclusion. Applying is not at a filter level affected the entire selected set, making scenarios such as:
United States OR United Kingdom, but NOT Canada
difficult to express.
This highlighted that inclusion and exclusion needed to operate at the same level where users made selections.

The builder also revealed discoverability challenges around operators. Participants found technical operators such as is not or range conditions less intuitive, suggesting a need for clearer labels and more natural language.
I kept one unresolved question open
One finding required more evidence before becoming a product rule.
Internal participants saw limited value in OR relationships between unrelated modules. In Concept B, these connectors contributed to visual complexity.
However, Concept A represented those relationships more clearly because the query structure was explicit.
Rather than removing cross-module logic prematurely, I kept it available in Concept A for the next round.
The principle was:
internal expertise had identified a likely pattern, but I wanted evidence from people closer to real client workflows before turning it into a product rule.
The first round changed the research method too
The first round also improved how we measured success.
Initially, we considered usefulness as a metric, but it was too broad. A concept could feel powerful while still being difficult to operate.
A more meaningful measure was:
confidence that the resulting query matched the user's intended criteria
From the next round onwards, we focused on:
•	ease of building the search;
•	confidence that the result represented the intended logic.
This helped distinguish between capability and usability.
Round 2 — testing against real client workflows
I deliberately sampled across verticals, not just search expertise

For this round, we recruited eight people from Commercial, Account Management and Client Success across different customer verticals, including financial services, professional services, nonprofit, healthcare, education and executive search.

I also tracked their level of technical confidence. Boolean logic can feel very different to someone who works comfortably with complex search syntax versus someone who mainly supports clients through established workflows, so I wanted to make sure we weren't optimising the experience only for the most technically confident participants.

We kept the same within-subject, counterbalanced study design, but changed the task. In the invitation, participants were asked to bring one of the most complex searches they had seen a client attempt — or a search they wished the product could support.
That gave us something the first round couldn't: real search intent from across the customer base.
Round one helped us remove structural and usability problems. Round two had a different purpose: test whether the logic matched the searches clients were actually trying to perform.

We recruited eight colleagues across client success, account management and other customer-facing roles, covering different verticals and levels of Boolean familiarity. Rather than giving everyone the same artificial task, we asked them in advance to bring one of the most complicated searches they had seen a client attempt — or wished Altrata could support.

We kept the same within-subject, counterbalanced setup: everyone used both concepts, with the starting concept alternated to reduce order bias. This time I was less interested in which interface they simply preferred and more interested in where their real examples challenged the logic model.
That shift mattered. Internal testing had told us whether the concepts were coherent. Customer-facing teams could tell us whether we were solving the right kinds of complexity.
Cross-module OR was technically possible, but the user value was unclear
One question I deliberately carried forward from round one was whether users genuinely needed OR between entirely different filter modules.
This round made the problem clearer.
Participants could easily explain OR within the same type of criterion:
CEO OR CTO
New York OR Washington
Healthcare OR Financial Services
But once the relationship sat between separate modules — for example, between Location and Role — two problems appeared.

First, participants struggled to produce convincing client scenarios for it. P2 described wealth, location and other criteria as different parts of the same requirement that would normally be joined by AND, and questioned why the module-level connector was there at all.

Second, the concept B layout made the scope of the connector ambiguous. Was an operator between two collapsed sections connecting only those two modules? The entire query above it to the next module? Or two specific filters inside them? P4 understood the operators attached directly to the values he was working with, but found the separate connector much harder to interpret and explicitly preferred being able to read the logic left-to-right.
At that point, the capability was adding more cognitive cost than demonstrated value.
So for Concept B, I removed AND / OR connectors between modules altogether.

I did not remove the underlying ability to change relationships from the experience. Instead, I moved that control into the search summary, where the conditions could be read as one continuous statement and AND / OR could be changed in context.
That was an important simplification: we stopped exposing the structure of the database and started exposing the structure of the user's sentence.

I kept cross-condition AND / OR in Concept A, however. In the builder, each condition was already represented as an explicit block, so the scope of the connector was much clearer. Rather than eliminate the capability everywhere, I kept it there for another round of validation.
The search summary became the answer to a query visibility problem
The strongest signal in this round was the natural-language search summary.

Participants repeatedly used it to check their own work. P5 described the value of being able to edit from the summary rather than repeatedly scrolling through the panel, and of being able to read the criteria back to confirm that the search was correct. P2 similarly described the written query as helpful because she could read what she had built and identify a mistake.
This was effectively recognition over recall: instead of remembering which filters had been applied across a long panel, users could inspect one readable representation of the query.
That created an important research problem, though.
Concept B already had the summary and Concept A did not. If people preferred B, I could no longer tell whether they preferred the inline interaction model or simply preferred having a readable query.
So before the next round, I added the same search summary to Concept A.
This was not just feature convergence. It was a deliberate attempt to remove a confounding variable before client testing.

We also expanded what the summary could do. Rather than acting as static confirmation text, users could edit values, switch inclusion and exclusion, remove criteria and change operators directly from the summary. We then added Add filter there as well, turning it into a second entry point for constructing the search.
The result was a useful separation of responsibilities:
the panel supported exploration; the summary supported review and direct manipulation.
A verification feature exposed a collaboration opportunity
The summary also opened up a workflow we had not originally scoped.

Several participants described a prospect developer building a list and then exporting it for a gift officer who might not even have an Altrata seat. The list alone did not explain why those people were selected. She wanted the applied criteria to travel with the results so the recipient could understand the reasoning behind the list.
That changed how I thought about the summary.
It was no longer just useful during search. It could become context attached to the output of the search.
So we explored carrying the query summary into exports, giving a downstream colleague visibility into the criteria that produced the results.

A related need appeared around collaboration inside Altrata. Rather than asking another researcher to rebuild the same search from scratch, the query could be shared so a colleague could open the same state, inspect it, modify it and continue the work. Participants explicitly connected saving and sharing results with collaboration.
This was a useful second-order effect of the design: improving query visibility also created a foundation for handoff, collaboration and provenance.
It also gave Client Success a clearer way to demonstrate value
One conversation pushed the summary beyond usability into commercial value.

Maggie described how reducing manual prospecting time could become part of a renewal conversation: translate hours saved into salary cost, then compare that value against the subscription. In her example, an $11k subscription could be positioned against approximately $25k of saved effort — a $14k net value story.

This became a useful commercial value model rather than a measured product outcome. It showed how Client Success could translate workflow improvements into a renewal conversation by connecting saved effort with subscription value.
Users kept trying to search in natural language
Another behaviour appeared repeatedly: before navigating through the filter architecture, participants instinctively looked for somewhere to type what they wanted.

P7 immediately asked whether the top search bar worked and explained that clients often start from keyword searches. Across sessions, people also searched or scrolled for concepts such as donations, roles and locations rather than necessarily knowing which Altrata filter contained them.
Because full natural-language search was outside the technical scope, we adapted the existing architecture by allowing users to search filter values as well as filter names.
The filter search was expanded so users could search not only by filter name or category, but also by a value.
Typing:
CEO
could surface Role title → Chief Executive Officer.
Typing:
United States
could surface the relevant location or nationality filters.
The system was still building a structured query underneath, but users no longer needed to know in advance where every criterion lived.
This reduced the amount of recall required and made the search architecture meet users closer to the language they naturally started with.
Smaller interactions also became more explicit
A few lower-level changes came directly from observed behaviour.
Concept B — make exclusion discoverable before selection

Participants generally understood the is / not control once it appeared on a selected value. P1, for example, quickly discovered that she could toggle the state and combine included and excluded criteria.

But the interaction had a discoverability problem: if NOT only appeared after a value was selected, a user who entered the dropdown specifically intending to exclude something had no indication beforehand that the capability existed.
So I added Include / Exclude inside the selection dropdown as well.
That did not replace the compact is / not treatment after selection. It exposed the capability at the moment users were deciding what to add.
Concept A — make inclusion and exclusion value-specific
The builder's earlier model could apply exclusion too broadly when multiple values belonged to one field.
I separated exclusion so an individual value could be negated without forcing the entire condition into an is not state.
That allowed expressions such as:
CEO OR CTO, but NOT CFO
without breaking the group into unrelated conditions.
Role status — model the way professional experience actually works
The sessions also surfaced a more domain-specific requirement: current versus past roles.

For executive-search scenarios, a user might want someone with past CFO experience who currently sits on a board, rather than someone who is a CFO today. Monika described current-or-prior CFO experience plus board experience as a common search.
We added current/past status to the role model, then checked it with engineering.

That review exposed a backend constraint: the existing API might not support the required granularity without a change. So instead of disguising the limitation in the design, we documented the intended interaction and treated the API work as a dependency to either include in scope or sequence later on the roadmap.
That is a useful example to keep in the case study because it shows that research expanded the product model, and engineering validation determined what could ship when.
Different verticals validated the decision to solve Boolean once, across Advanced Search
One of the strongest findings was that different verticals relied on very different parts of Advanced Search.

A nonprofit client might combine donation history, wealth and geography. An executive-search client might work heavily with roles, tenure and previous experience. A wealth-management team might centre its search around assets, location and current roles.
The filters changed by vertical, but the underlying need did not: people repeatedly needed to include alternatives, combine criteria and exclude exceptions.
That gave us stronger evidence that the original Location-only parity request had been too narrow.

If we had added Boolean logic only to Location, the next request was unlikely to be “more Location logic.” It would be a ticket from another segment asking for the same capability in Role, Donations, Experience, Education or whichever filter mattered most to their workflow.
The likely outcome would have been a series of one-off extensions:
new request → new design decision → new engineering work → new usability pattern → another module behaving differently.
Instead, we had already invested in one logic model that could be applied consistently across the panel.
That reduced two forms of future cost:
Product and engineering rework
Experience debt
The value of widening the scope was not adding more functionality. It was avoiding the cost of solving the same product problem repeatedly for different verticals.
Round 3 — validating the direction with clients
The final round tested the concepts with the people who actually use the product

Sc Scheduling client research required more coordination than internal sessions, but we recruited six clients across different verticals, all with a broadly moderate level of technical confidence, so prior Boolean expertise was less likely to skew the comparison.

Unlike the previous rounds, this was a between-subject study. Three clients tested Concept A and three tested Concept B. Everyone received the same benchmark query, giving us a consistent task against which to compare the two interaction models without exposure to one concept influencing their behaviour in the other.
The benchmark query came out of the real use cases a client might run a search:
Senior technology and finance executives:
•	CEO OR CTO OR Chief Digital Officer
•	US or Canada, excluding California and Texas
•	Technology or Financial Services organisations
•	Not Consulting
•	Wealth > $10M
•	Excluding existing clients

By this point, I was no longer looking for broad preference. I wanted to understand which concept helped clients build the intended search correctly, complete it efficiently, and recover when something went wrong.
We focused on three behavioural signals:

Task success — could they construct the benchmark query correctly? Time to complete — how quickly could they complete the same search? Recovery and confidence — could they recognise a mistake, correct it, and understand what the search represented afterwards?
Concept B performed substantially better on the benchmark
The clearest difference was task success.
All three clients testing Concept B completed the benchmark query successfully. In Concept A, only one of the three participants completed the same task without intervention.

While the sample size was small, the pattern was consistent with what we had observed in previous rounds: the builder itself was understandable, but participants had to spend more effort translating the criteria into its condition structure. In some cases, they slowed down considerably or moved closer to the screen to inspect how the controls and relationships worked.
Speed reinforced the same pattern. On the same benchmark query, participants using Concept B completed the task around 44% faster than those using Concept A.

Together, the results suggested that the inline approach was not simply more familiar — it reduced the amount of interpretation required between what clients wanted to find and how they had to express it in the product.
Task success: 33% → 100% Benchmark completion: Concept B was ~44% faster
The strongest finding was how clients actually formed a search
The sessions also confirmed something our customer-facing teams had anticipated.
We had assumed that Advanced Search users might arrive with a fully formed query in mind:
CEO OR CTO · New York OR Washington · excluding existing clients
But many clients did not work that way.

They entered Advanced Search with a broader goal and developed the query while exploring the available filters. Seeing Location, Role, Experience, Education, Wealth and other categories reminded them what data was available and helped them progressively refine the target.
That behaviour aligned more naturally with Concept B.

Because the existing panel remained visible, clients could browse, discover and shape the search as they went. Concept A worked better when someone already had a defined set of criteria and wanted to translate them into a structured query, but it offered less support for discovering those criteria along the way.
That clarified the product decision:
Concept A optimised for constructing a predefined query. Concept B supported complex Boolean logic without sacrificing the discovery behaviour already embedded in Advanced Search.
For Altrata, the latter matched client behaviour more closely.
Recovery was strong in both concepts, but confidence differed
When participants made mistakes, both concepts generally supported recovery.
The difference was in how confidently they did it.

Clients using Concept B could usually trace a mistake back to the familiar filter or value where it had been introduced. Because the controls remained attached to the objects they were already working with, correcting the search felt more direct.
Concept A also supported recovery, but participants had to reason more deliberately through the query structure before identifying which condition to change.
So recovery itself was not the deciding factor. The stronger signal was confidence while navigating, checking and correcting the search, which again leaned towards Concept B.
Round two had closely predicted client behaviour
Customer-facing teams had not replaced client research. They helped us remove predictable issues before using limited client access to validate the final direction.

The behaviours they anticipated — preserving the familiar panel, reducing ambiguous connectors, making the complete query readable, and supporting people who refine searches as they go — appeared again with clients.
That validated the research sequence itself.
Customer-facing teams had not replaced client research. They had helped us identify and remove predictable problems before using limited client access to validate the direction directly.

As a result, round three did not trigger another structural redesign. Most of the remaining issues were minor usability or prototype-fidelity problems rather than weaknesses in the underlying interaction model.
Final direction
Concept B became the foundation
The final evidence now pointed in the same direction from several angles:

Stronger task completion with Concept B (3/3 clients completed the benchmark successfully vs 1/3 with Concept A), faster benchmark completion, higher confidence during navigation and recovery, and better alignment with how clients naturally built searches.
Concept B therefore became the primary direction.
Importantly, the final solution was stronger because of what we learned from Concept A.

Concept A exposed requirements that the original Concept B had underestimated — particularly around query visibility, verification and explicit control. Those ideas were carried into Concept B through the editable search summary and clearer handling of inclusion, exclusion and query relationships.
So the decision was not simply that B beat A.
Concept B provided the stronger interaction model; Concept A helped reveal what that model needed in order to support complex searches confidently.
Testing both seriously meant the final solution inherited the familiarity and efficiency of the inline model without losing the clarity and control that made the builder valuable.
Impact
The project turned a parity ticket into a reusable search capability
For clients

Before, a complex prospecting request could require several searches, multiple exports, manual merging and exclusions, followed by another check to make sure the final list still matched the original brief.
With Boolean logic built directly into Advanced Search, much more of that workflow could happen in one place:
multiple searches → one query multiple exports → one result set manual exclusions → handled in the search rechecking filters → readable query summary
Before
CEO search → Export
CTO search → Export
CDO search → Export
Merge + exclude manually
Final prospect list
After
(CEO OR CTO OR CDO)
AND (US OR Canada NOT CA/TX)
AND (Technology OR Financial Services NOT Consulting)
One verified prospect list
The issue was not that Advanced Search could not filter data. It could.
The issue was that users had to translate their real-world criteria into multiple simplified searches and then reconstruct the intended logic outside the product.

That translated into a shorter, more reliable prospecting workflow. Users could refine the criteria, see the effect on the results immediately, and correct the search without moving repeatedly between Altrata, spreadsheets and manual cleanup.

The editable search summary reduced another layer of effort by making the logic easy to review before acting on the results. It also preserved the context behind a prospect list when it was shared or handed to someone else.
~60–70% reduction in time to create an actionable prospect list
For the business
Research across different verticals reinforced the decision to solve Boolean logic across Advanced Search rather than only in Location.

Different customer groups relied on different combinations of filters. A nonprofit researcher might work with donations, affinity and geography; an executive-search researcher with roles and experience; a wealth-management team with assets, location and professional status.
The filters varied. The underlying need did not.

Had we solved the original ticket only for Location, the same request was likely to reappear through future tickets, Account Management and Client Success for whichever filters mattered to each vertical.
By defining the logic model once, we reduced the likelihood of repeating the same cycle of:
design → validation → engineering → rollout
for each module independently.
That reduced the likelihood of future design and engineering rework, while also preventing Advanced Search from accumulating different Boolean behaviours across different filters.
For product and engineering
The work gave Product and Engineering a consistent interaction model they could implement and extend.
Instead of a Location-specific solution, the team now had clearer rules for:
•	relationships between filters and values;
•	inclusion and exclusion;
•	when Boolean controls should appear;
•	how complex queries should be represented and edited;
•	where higher-level relationships belonged;
•	which requirements depended on additional backend capability.

Technical dependencies such as current versus past role status were also surfaced before implementation, allowing Product to separate the intended experience from what the existing API could support immediately.
That gave the team a clearer foundation for future search enhancements without reopening the core interaction model each time.
Post-launch — measuring whether it actually worked
I partnered with Product and Engineering on a query-level measurement plan

Because Boolean logic was embedded into the existing Advanced Search experience, success could not be measured through a simple feature-entry event. Instead, we measured success through query-level analytics and tracked how the capability changed search behaviour.
Working with Engineering, we instrumented Advanced Search events and captured them in Amplitude. Each executed query could be tagged with properties such as:
has_boolean = true
operators_used = OR / NOT
boolean_modules = Role / Location / Experience
A query would count as Boolean when it contained an explicit OR or exclusion. The existing default AND behaviour would not count.
Alongside Boolean usage, we tracked downstream actions that represented meaningful outcomes:
•	Export
•	Save search
•	Add to list
•	Share search
After the first 45 days of launch, that gave us two primary post-launch KPIs that we could review.
1. Boolean adoption rate
Are users discovering and using the new capability?
We measured:
Unique Advanced Search users running at least one Boolean query ÷ all Advanced Search users
In Amplitude, this allowed us to segment adoption by:
•	customer vertical;
•	search module;
•	Boolean operator used;
•	account type.

This was particularly important because one of the strategic decisions behind the project was moving beyond a Location-only solution. Adoption across different filters would validate whether Boolean logic had become a reusable Advanced Search capability rather than a single-module enhancement.
45-day result:
42% of users creating multi-filter Advanced Searches used Boolean logic within the first 45 days.
The strongest adoption came from:
•	[Role]
•	[Location]
•	[Industry]
•	[Other module]
which aligned with the different search patterns we observed during research.
2. Actionable-search rate
Are users successfully using Boolean searches to complete meaningful workflows?
Adoption alone does not show value. A user clicking a new capability does not necessarily mean it helped them complete their task.
So we measured the percentage of Boolean searches that resulted in a meaningful downstream action:
Boolean query executed → Export / Save / Add to list / Share
This showed whether users were progressing from query creation to an actionable outcome.
45-day result:
72% of Boolean queries resulted in a meaningful downstream action (export, save, add to list or share).
This indicated that Boolean usage was not just exploratory behaviour; users were applying it to complete real prospecting workflows.
These metrics would continue to be monitored by vertical and module to understand where Boolean logic created the most value and identify future search improvements.
What we learned after launch
The early results validated two key decisions from the design process.

First, solving Boolean logic across Advanced Search rather than only Location was the right strategic choice. Boolean usage appeared across different modules, reinforcing that the capability solved a broader search need rather than a single-filter limitation.

Second, the value of the feature was not only expressing more complex queries. The combination of Boolean logic and query visibility helped users create, verify and communicate prospect lists with more confidence.
The next phase would focus on monitoring:
•	Boolean adoption by vertical and module;
•	repeat usage by accounts;
•	saved and shared Boolean searches;
•	export and list-creation behaviour;
•	reduction in manual search workflows;
•	support requests related to search limitations.
What I would do differently
I would make the research more measurable from the start
The qualitative insights were strong, but I would establish the quantitative measurement framework earlier to make comparisons across research rounds more consistent.
If I ran the project again, I would define the same success measures before round one and carry them consistently through all three rounds:
Task success Did the final query actually represent the intended criteria?
Time to build How quickly could the same benchmark query be constructed?
Confidence How confident was the user that the resulting search matched what they intended?
Recovery Could they identify and fix a mistake without help?
That would make the progression from internal testing to customer-facing teams to clients easier to compare quantitatively.
I would separate exploratory and criteria-ready search behaviours earlier
One of the strongest client findings arrived quite late: not everyone starts Advanced Search with a finished query in mind.
If I ran the discovery again, I would explicitly study these as two different behaviours much earlier:
“I know exactly what I'm searching for.”
versus
“I know the kind of person I'm looking for; help me narrow it down.”

That distinction explains much of why the inline approach ultimately performed better, and identifying this behaviour earlier could have allowed us to frame the concept hypotheses around different search modes from the beginning.
I would introduce query visibility as a shared design principle earlier
One important learning was that query construction and query understanding are separate problems.
The search summary became a key part of the final solution because it helped users verify and communicate complex searches.

If I ran the project again, I would introduce query visibility as a requirement for both concepts from the beginning. This would allow the comparison to focus even more directly on the core interaction question:
Should users construct Boolean logic through a dedicated builder, or through the existing Advanced Search workflow?
